distribution: Worldwide; predominant in the Great Plains (USA), Australia, and most wheat-growing regions

vector.name: Wheat curl mite
vector.notes: Mites are slow crawlers, disperse mainly by wind, and can transmit the virus between wheat and corn

symptoms: Streaks of yellowed, non-uniform discoloration on leaves
Severe infections can cause 100% crop loss
Symptoms often more severe when synergistic infections occur with Triticum mosaic virus or High plains virus
disease_cycle: Virus overwinters in grasses and cereal crops and in infected seeds
Wheat curl mites acquire virus from infected plants and transmit it to healthy plants
Mites depend on wind to move between plants and fields
Volunteer wheat and grassy weeds act as reservoirs for both mites and virus
Multiple generations of mites per season can amplify spread
conditions_for_development: Warm weather favors mite reproduction and virus transmission
Availability of volunteer wheat or grassy hosts increases disease prevalence
Early planting increases risk due to longer exposure to mites

cultural: Destroy volunteer wheat at least 2 weeks before planting new winter wheat
Avoid early planting to reduce exposure to mites
Select wheat varieties with lower susceptibility to WSMV
chemical: Miticides are not effective against the wheat curl mite for controlling virus spread
resistance: Use resistant/tolerant wheat cultivars where available
Research on RNAi-based resistance is ongoing

impact: Yield losses can reach up to 100% in susceptible varieties
Co-infection with other viruses can exacerbate damage
references: Seifers DL et al., 2002. Wheat streak mosaic virus: An Overview. Plant Disease 86: 781–790.
Martinez et al., 2019. Wheat curl mite-virus interactions. Front. Plant Sci.
USDA-ARS research on WSMV and vector biology.
